narrativeReportMd:
# CareTeam R4 to R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
Breaking changes were found for local CareTeam content. Existing R4 instances can fail R6 validation because `CareTeam.encounter`, `CareTeam.reasonCode`, `CareTeam.reasonReference`, and `CareTeam.participant.period` are no longer valid element names, and because `CareTeam.participant.role` was narrowed from repeating to single-valued. R6 also introduces content that R4 cannot faithfully carry, especially participant `effectiveTiming`, `supportingInfo`, and broader participant reference targets.

## Scope
The comparison used the supplied R4 and R6 CareTeam StructureDefinitions plus related local ValueSet, CodeSystem, CodeableReference, and Encounter definitions. Inherited Resource/DomainResource/Element changes are explicitly excluded from findings.

## Main migration themes
The largest migration theme is representation change: several R4 sibling elements are removed or folded into newer R6 patterns (`CodeableReference` and choice elements). A second theme is participant modeling: participant roles are now one-per-participant, participant availability uses `effective[x]`, and references can point to more kinds of entities. A third theme is reverse-link migration for encounter context: preserving old `CareTeam.encounter` may require updating R6 Encounter resources rather than only transforming CareTeam resources.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-impact R4-to-R6 breaks are the removed `encounter` field, the `reasonCode`/`reasonReference` merge into `reason`, the `participant.period` replacement with `participant.effective[x]`, and the `participant.role` maximum cardinality decrease. These affect validators, generated model classes, serializers, FHIRPath queries, and downstream analytics that expect the R4 element names or cardinalities.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most useful for deciding how to preserve removed encounter context, how to split multi-role participants without changing business meaning, and whether the example ValueSet composition changes should affect local coding policy. Terminology expansion was not available, so the exact practical effect of example binding changes is uncertain.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Several changes could have been made less disruptive by keeping old elements as deprecated aliases, adding optional new elements, or expressing new rules as profiles. The R6 design is internally coherent, especially around `CodeableReference` and richer participant modeling, but cross-version migration needs explicit transforms.

## Follow-up analysis
Follow-up should include the Encounter report for `Encounter.careTeam`, the CodeableReference datatype report, and terminology expansion review for LOINC and SNOMED CT example bindings.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: CareTeam has material local breaking changes from R4 to R6. The top migration concerns are removed/renamed CareTeam elements, the `participant.role` repeatability narrowing, and R6 participant/reason content that R4 cannot fully represent. Confidence is high for structural deltas and medium for terminology impact because full expansions were not performed.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration is mostly a structural transform rather than a simple version-label update. R4 `reasonCode` and `reasonReference` should be converted into R6 `reason` CodeableReference entries; R4 `participant.period` should become `participant.effectivePeriod`; participants with multiple roles should be split; and old `encounter` links need a policy, potentially updating R6 `Encounter.careTeam`. R6-to-R4 conversion needs loss rules for `effectiveTiming`, `supportingInfo`, broader participant references, and CodeableReference entries that carry both concept and reference.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for element presence, cardinality, reference target, constraint, and required status-code conclusions because they come directly from the local StructureDefinitions and CodeSystem/ValueSet files. Confidence is medium for example-bound terminology impact because SNOMED CT and LOINC expansions were not available, and medium for change justification because official diff narrative or issue history was not supplied.

findings.title: CareTeam.encounter was removed from the CareTeam resource

oldState.summary: R4 had optional `CareTeam.encounter` as `0..1 Reference(Encounter)` and marked it summary.

semanticText.definition: The Encounter during which this CareTeam was created or to which the creation of this record is tightly associated.
semanticText.comment: This will typically be the encounter the event occurred within, but some activities may be initiated prior to or after the official completion of an encounter but still be tied to the context of the encounter.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 CareTeam could directly state the Encounter that created the CareTeam or was tightly associated with the record.

newState.narrativeMd: The R6 CareTeam snapshot and differential omit `CareTeam.encounter`. The related R6 Encounter resource has `Encounter.careTeam`, but that is a reverse link on another resource, not a CareTeam element.

facts.note: No corresponding CareTeam element exists in R6.
R6 Encounter has a reverse reference to CareTeam; this requires cross-resource migration.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: No same-path R6 CareTeam element exists. The only plausible related model found locally is R6 `Encounter.careTeam`, which reverses the direction and lives on Encounter.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct old-valid/new-invalid break: an R4 CareTeam containing `encounter` has an unknown element under the R6 CareTeam structure. Generated R6 classes, JSON/XML serializers, FHIRPath expressions, and validators will not accept or expose the field. The business impact can be high when encounter context is used to scope team membership or audit provenance.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Dropping encounter context can weaken episode/visit-specific interpretation of a care team and can affect clinical workflow, reporting, or audit trails.

justification.inferredGoal: Move encounter-to-care-team linkage to Encounter or avoid duplicating contextual links on CareTeam.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain optional or deprecated `CareTeam.encounter` while adding `Encounter.careTeam` and guidance on the authoritative link.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Moving encounter/team allocation toward `Encounter.careTeam` is a reasonable modeling goal, but complete removal of `CareTeam.encounter` invalidates existing R4 instances that carried encounter context. The available definitions show the new reverse link but do not show why retaining the old optional field for a transition would fail the R6 goal. Because the compatibility-preserving design has real consistency costs but is plausible, the break is not clearly justified rather than clearly necessary.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base R6 design could have kept `CareTeam.encounter` as optional and deprecated while adding or encouraging `Encounter.careTeam`, with narrative or invariants specifying which side is authoritative when both are present. That would preserve most R4 wire instances. The material tradeoff is duplicate cross-resource linkage: systems could disagree about whether the Encounter or the CareTeam is the source of truth, and reconciliation logic could persist indefinitely.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 instances but creates bidirectional encounter-team links that need reconciliation.

evidence.detail: R4 defines `CareTeam.encounter` as `0..1 Reference(Encounter)`.
evidence.quote: The Encounter during which this CareTeam was created or to which the creation of this record is tightly associated.

evidence.detail: No R6 CareTeam element with path `CareTeam.encounter` is present.
R6 Encounter has `Encounter.careTeam` as `0..* Reference(CareTeam)`, a possible cross-resource migration target.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example is illustrative. Preserving the link in R6 likely requires updating the referenced Encounter, which is not possible when only a standalone CareTeam instance is transformed.

findings.narrativeMd: `CareTeam.encounter` disappeared from the CareTeam content model. Existing R4 instances that use the field will not validate as R6 CareTeam resources, and application code that indexes or displays care teams by encounter will lose its direct field unless a cross-resource strategy is implemented.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 instance with `CareTeam.encounter` is old-valid/new-invalid under the R6 CareTeam StructureDefinition because the element is absent. This affects strict JSON/XML parsers, generated model classes, validators, FHIRPath queries such as `CareTeam.encounter`, and summary searches or projections that depended on the field. R6-to-R4 is not the primary direction for this finding because the R6 CareTeam resource no longer has a same-resource encounter field.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory R4 CareTeam records with `encounter`. If the corresponding Encounter resources are available and controlled by the migration, consider adding `Encounter.careTeam` references in R6 and removing `CareTeam.encounter`. If Encounter resources are not available, preserve the association with a version-specific extension or external mapping table and flag records for review. Test standalone and bundled migrations because this is a cross-resource transform.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The removal was probably avoidable at the wire-format level: an optional deprecated field could have preserved R4 instances while steering new systems toward Encounter-based linkage. The tradeoff is that FHIR would carry two possible linkage directions, increasing synchronization burden.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Confirm with official R6 narrative or change notes whether `Encounter.careTeam` is intended as the normative migration target.

findings.title: CareTeam.reasonCode and reasonReference were merged into CareTeam.reason CodeableReference

oldState.summary: R4 represented reasons as two repeating sibling arrays: `reasonCode` (`CodeableConcept`) and `reasonReference` (`Reference(Condition)`).

semanticText.definition: R4 `reasonCode` describes why the care team exists; R4 `reasonReference` identifies Condition(s) that the care team addresses.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 split coded reasons and Condition references into separate arrays. A single CareTeam could carry any number of codes and any number of Condition references independently.

newState.summary: R6 uses repeating `CareTeam.reason` with type `CodeableReference` targeted to Condition and the same example clinical-findings binding.

semanticText.definition: Describes why the care team exists.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 folds both representations into `reason`, where each CodeableReference can hold a `concept`, a `reference`, or both.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The old and new elements have the same short text for why the care team exists, keep the clinical-findings example binding for coded content, and preserve Condition as the reference target.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 field names `reasonCode` and `reasonReference` are absent in R6, so existing instances using them become invalid without transformation. Runtime risk is high for generated R4 clients, serializers, and FHIRPath expressions. R6-to-R4 risk is medium because most R6 CodeableReference entries can be split into R4 code/reference arrays, but an R6 entry containing both a concept and a reference loses their explicit pairing in R4.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Reasons can drive clinical interpretation and filtering; lossy or dropped reasons can affect care-team selection and review.

justification.inferredGoal: Adopt the newer CodeableReference pattern that allows a reason to be represented by concept, reference, or both in a single element.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Add `CareTeam.reason` CodeableReference while temporarily retaining deprecated `reasonCode` and `reasonReference`.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal is strong: `CodeableReference` lets a reason be a concept, a Condition reference, or both as one item, avoiding the R4 parallel-array pattern. Keeping the old siblings would preserve R4 instances, but it would not fully meet the pairing and simplification goal and could leave implementers with two same-resource ways to express the same reason. Those material ambiguity and long-term cleanup costs make the breaking merge probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking design would add `CareTeam.reason` and keep `reasonCode` and `reasonReference` as deprecated aliases for a transition, possibly with warnings against using old and new forms together. This would make simple R4 data valid without transformation. The tradeoff is validation and semantic ambiguity: old split arrays cannot preserve an R6 concept/reference pair, and deprecated duplicate fields might remain in production indefinitely.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Reduces immediate wire breakage but leaves duplicate reason representations and conflict rules.

evidence.detail: R4 defines `reasonCode` as `0..* CodeableConcept` with example clinical-findings binding.
R4 defines `reasonReference` as `0..* Reference(Condition)`.
R6 defines `reason` as `0..* CodeableReference` targeted to Condition with example clinical-findings binding.
R6 CodeableReference contains optional `concept` and `reference` children.

examples.examplesMd: The R6-to-R4 example can be split into R4 `reasonCode` and `reasonReference`, but R4 cannot preserve that the concept and reference were intentionally paired in one CodeableReference item.

findings.narrativeMd: The reason representation changed from two R4 arrays to one R6 CodeableReference array. This is more than a rename in generated code: transforms must move data into nested `concept` or `reference` children and decide how to handle entries that carry both.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances containing `reasonCode` or `reasonReference` are invalid against R6 CareTeam until transformed. R6 instances using `reason.concept` or `reason.reference` are generally representable in R4, but paired concept/reference semantics and any CodeableReference-level extensions may not be preserved by splitting into two independent R4 arrays.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map each R4 `reasonCode` item to an R6 `reason` item with `concept`. Map each R4 `reasonReference` item to an R6 `reason` item with `reference`. For R6-to-R4, split simple entries back to the corresponding R4 arrays and flag entries containing both concept and reference, extensions, or ordering-sensitive semantics for review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The CodeableReference merge is cleaner long term, but it could have been introduced as an additive element with deprecated old siblings for one transition cycle. That would reduce wire-format breakage while leaving temporary duplication and conflict-resolution rules.

findings.title: CareTeam.participant.role maximum cardinality decreased from many to one

oldState.summary: R4 allowed each participant to have `0..*` role CodeableConcepts.

semanticText.definition: Indicates specific responsibility of an individual within the care team, such as Primary care physician or caregiver.

oldState.narrativeMd: One R4 participant backbone could carry multiple roles for the same member.

newState.summary: R6 allows at most one `role` per participant and tells users to create multiple participants for multiple roles.

semanticText.comment: If a participant has multiple roles within the team, then there should be multiple participants.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 normalizes multiple roles by requiring separate participant repetitions rather than multiple role repetitions inside one participant.

facts.newValue: split participant repetitions when more than one role exists

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The path and meaning are unchanged; only maximum cardinality and clarifying comment changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct validation break for any R4 participant with two or more role values. Generated R6 classes may expose a single role instead of an array, and business logic that treats roles as a set on one participant must be refactored to handle multiple participant repetitions.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Incorrectly dropping secondary roles can change who is understood to have responsibility in the team.

justification.inferredGoal: Make each participant repetition represent one member-role participation and avoid ambiguous role-specific metadata.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `participant.role` repeating but add best-practice guidance or a warning to split multiple roles into multiple participant entries.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: R6 explicitly states that a participant with multiple roles should be represented by multiple participant repetitions. That goal becomes more important with participant-level `effective[x]` and `supportingInfo`, because timing and supporting documentation can be role-specific. A non-breaking warning would preserve old data but only partially achieve the normalized one-role participation model. Given those material semantics, the max-cardinality break is probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could have left `role` as `0..*` and added a warning invariant, comment, or profiling guidance that multiple roles SHOULD be split. This would keep all R4 instances valid. Its weakness is that base R6 instances could still put several roles on one participant, making it unclear whether `effective[x]`, `onBehalfOf`, extensions, and `supportingInfo` apply to every role or only some roles.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves R4 multi-role participants but cannot enforce one role per participant and leaves role-specific metadata ambiguous.

evidence.detail: R4 maximum cardinality is `*`.
R6 maximum cardinality is `1`.
R6 comment says participants with multiple roles should be represented by multiple participants.

examples.examplesMd: The R6 migration duplicates participant-level data for each role. Implementers should preserve extensions, member, onBehalfOf, effective, and supportingInfo consistently when splitting.

findings.narrativeMd: `CareTeam.participant.role` changed from a list to a single value. The R6 model expects separate participant repetitions for multiple roles. This can alter application assumptions because identity of a participant is no longer simply member plus an array of roles; member-role participation becomes the unit.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Any R4 participant with more than one `role` value is invalid in R6. R6-to-R4 is representable because R4 can carry one role or many, but round-tripping a split R6 representation through R4 aggregation can accidentally merge participant repetitions if migration code deduplicates by member alone.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Search for participant repetitions with more than one role. Split them into one R6 participant per role, copying shared fields and preserving role-specific extensions where possible. Regression tests should include multi-role participants with extensions, periods/effective values, and onBehalfOf references to ensure no role is dropped.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The normalization goal is understandable, particularly once R6 adds participant `effective[x]` and `supportingInfo`, but a mandatory cardinality decrease in the base resource is hard breaking. A best-practice invariant would have avoided invalidating existing R4 data.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Review local business rules that identify duplicate participants by member only; they may collapse the intended R6 split representation.

findings.title: CareTeam.participant.period was replaced by participant.effective[x]

oldState.summary: R4 used optional `participant.period` with type Period.

semanticText.definition: Indicates when the specific member or organization did (or is intended to) come into effect and end.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 participant availability/effective time was represented only as a Period under the field name `period`.

newState.summary: R6 uses optional choice `participant.effective[x]` with Period or Timing.

semanticText.short: When the member is generally available within this care team
semanticText.definition: When the member is generally available within this care team.
semanticText.comment: This is populated while creating / managing the CareTeam to ensure there is coverage when servicing CarePlan activities from the Schedule.
semanticText.requirements: To manage members who share the same role, but with different timing.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 changes both the element name and the domain. Period remains available as `effectivePeriod`, and recurring availability can be represented as `effectiveTiming`.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The old and new elements occupy the same participant time/availability role, and R6 retains Period while adding Timing and changing the name to `effective[x]`.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances with `participant.period` contain an element name that R6 no longer defines; R6 generated classes and JSON serializers will use choice-specific names such as `effectivePeriod` or `effectiveTiming`. R6 `effectiveTiming` cannot be represented losslessly in R4, which only had a simple Period.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Participant timing can determine coverage expectations; losing recurring schedules can change operational interpretation.

justification.inferredGoal: Support richer participant availability, including recurring schedules, and clarify semantics as general availability.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain `participant.period` and add a separate optional Timing or availability element instead of replacing it with `effective[x]`.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 requirement for recurring or schedule-like availability is substantive, and a choice element is a clean way to say the effective availability can be either a `Period` or a `Timing`. A less-breaking additive design exists, but it would leave two related participant timing fields and require rules for whether they can coexist. Because those tradeoffs are material, the rename to `effective[x]` is probably justified despite the field-name break.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A base R6 alternative could keep `participant.period` for the R4 case and add `participant.timing` or `participant.availabilityTiming` for recurring schedules. Existing R4 instances would remain valid. The cost is a less coherent model than `effective[x]`: implementers would need to handle both fields, decide precedence when both are present, and accept that FHIRPath and generated APIs expose separate timing concepts rather than one choice.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves existing Period wire names but creates two timing fields and one-of-many usage rules.

evidence.detail: R4 defines `participant.period` as `0..1 Period`.
R6 defines `participant.effective[x]` as `0..1` with types Period and Timing.

examples.examplesMd: The old Period maps cleanly to `effectivePeriod`; `effectiveTiming` needs a lossy approximation or extension when converting back to R4.

findings.narrativeMd: `participant.period` did not simply gain an alias; it was replaced by a choice element. That affects wire names, generated property names, FHIRPath paths, and transform logic. The new Timing option is useful but introduces R6 data that R4 cannot carry natively.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with `participant.period` are invalid in R6 because R6 expects `effectivePeriod` for a Period choice value. R6 instances with `effectivePeriod` can be mapped back to R4 `period`, but `effectiveTiming` is not R4-representable without losing recurrence detail or using an extension.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map R4 `participant.period` to R6 `participant.effectivePeriod`. Update code, FHIRPath, and search/extraction logic to use `effective[x]` choice handling. For R6-to-R4, map `effectivePeriod` back to `period`; for `effectiveTiming`, define a cross-version extension or a policy for deriving a coarse Period and flagging the record as lossy.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change could have been less disruptive by preserving `period` and adding Timing separately. The R6 choice design is cleaner but creates a field-name break for all existing Period users.

findings.title: Participant member and onBehalfOf reference domains were widened and onBehalfOf semantics changed

oldState.summary: R4 `member` targeted Practitioner, PractitionerRole, RelatedPerson, Patient, Organization, or CareTeam; `onBehalfOf` targeted only Organization and had error invariant ctm-1 tying it to Practitioner members.

constraints.human: CareTeam.participant.onBehalfOf can only be populated when CareTeam.participant.member is a Practitioner

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 treated `onBehalfOf` narrowly as the organization of a practitioner and constrained it accordingly.

newState.summary: R6 `member` adds Group and HealthcareService; `onBehalfOf` expands to the same broad participant target set. R6 removes ctm-1 and adds warning ctm-2 that a participant should have role or member.

semanticText.comment: Using Group is only allowed when the group represents a family or a household and should not represent groups of Practitioners.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 broadens participant modeling so members and represented entities can include groups and services, and `onBehalfOf` is no longer limited to an organization acting for a practitioner.

facts.oldValue: ctm-1 error: onBehalfOf only when member is Practitioner

facts.newValue: ctm-2 warning: role or member exists

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The same paths exist in both versions, but targetProfiles and local participant invariants changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4-valid references remain valid in R6, so this is not an R4-to-R6 instance break. The risk is in R6-to-R4 conversion and runtime assumptions: R6 instances can point `member` or `onBehalfOf` to resource types that strict R4 profiles do not allow, and code that assumed `onBehalfOf` is an Organization may mis-handle broader references.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Misinterpreting a group, service, or patient as an organization could affect responsibility and authorization workflows.

justification.inferredGoal: Model care-team participants and represented parties more broadly, including family/household groups and healthcare services.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: The target-domain widening preserves R4-valid references, so no less-breaking R4-to-R6 base alternative is needed.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Broadening `member` and `onBehalfOf` supports a more expressive participant/proxy model, and the old R4 reference targets remain allowed. The change can still affect generated code and business logic that assumed `onBehalfOf` was only an Organization, but it is not an old-valid/new-invalid base instance break. Under the calibration rules, target-domain widening that preserves R4 instances is not a case where a backward-compatible alternative is applicable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Keeping `onBehalfOf` narrowly Organization-only and adding extensions, profiles, or a separate represented-entity element would be a different design, but it is not needed to preserve R4 wire instances because those instances already remain valid in R6. Such approaches would mainly mitigate R6-to-R4 conversion or old runtime assumptions, so they should not be counted as a `Yes` or `Partial` base compatibility alternative.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R6-to-R4 conversion and old type assumptions need migration policies, not a less-breaking R6 base design.

evidence.detail: R4 member target profiles are Practitioner, PractitionerRole, RelatedPerson, Patient, Organization, and CareTeam.
R6 member adds Group and HealthcareService.
R4 onBehalfOf is Reference(Organization) with R4 ctm-1 on the participant backbone.
R6 onBehalfOf targets the broad participant set and has proxy/agent/representative semantics.
R6 adds a warning that role or member should exist.

examples.examplesMd: This R6 participant is valid against the R6 target-profile list but cannot be represented as a strict R4 CareTeam participant because R4 does not allow HealthcareService as member or Group as onBehalfOf.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 expands who can be a participant and who a participant can act on behalf of. This is forward-looking and more expressive, but it changes the contract for systems that used R4 target profiles as type guarantees. The removed R4 invariant also means `onBehalfOf` no longer implies a practitioner/organization relationship.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: No common R4-valid instance becomes invalid from these reference target changes alone. In the reverse direction, R6 instances with Group or HealthcareService references fail strict R4 validation. Runtime code that casts `onBehalfOf` to Organization or uses the presence of `onBehalfOf` as evidence of a practitioner affiliation needs updates.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update generated reference target validation, UI labels, authorization checks, and downstream analytics to handle Group and HealthcareService. For R6-to-R4 conversion, define explicit policies: reject unsupported references, preserve them in extensions, or map them to Organization only when a safe business mapping exists. Do not silently coerce Group or HealthcareService to Organization.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The broadened participant model could have been expressed with an additive element, but R6 chose to generalize existing paths. That improves consistency while making old type assumptions unsafe.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: The R6 Group limitation is in comment text, not an invariant; local profiles may need to enforce the family/household restriction if it matters.

findings.title: CareTeam.participant.supportingInfo was added with no R4 equivalent

oldState.summary: R4 had no participant-level supportingInfo element.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 participant could carry extensions, but no standard field for documentation supporting the participant role.

newState.summary: R6 adds `participant.supportingInfo` as `0..* Reference(Resource)` and marks it summary.

semanticText.definition: The basis for the member's role participation in care team. For example, supporting documentation that establishes legal power of attorney or court ordered guardianship.
semanticText.comment: Enables care providers a more efficient path to review the participation, if necessary.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 can point from a participant to arbitrary supporting resources such as legal authority or guardianship documentation.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element is new in R6 and has no same-purpose standard R4 CareTeam field.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Optional additions do not invalidate R4 instances when moving to R6. The risk is reverse conversion and downstream consumers: R6 supporting documentation cannot be carried in a standard R4 CareTeam element, and dropping it may remove legally or operationally important context.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: If used for power of attorney, guardianship, or court-ordered participation, loss of supportingInfo can affect consent, authorization, or care coordination review.

justification.inferredGoal: Provide a standard place to link documentation justifying a participant role.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Optional additive R6 content does not break R4-to-R6 base validation.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: `participant.supportingInfo` adds an optional standard place for documentation supporting participation, such as legal authority or guardianship. R4 CareTeam instances remain valid because they simply omit the new element. The compatibility concern is R6-to-R4 loss, not an R4-to-R6 breaking base design, so the addition is justified and the alternative question is not applicable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No less-breaking R6 base design is needed for preserving R4 instances. A shared extension for R4 exchange could help mixed-version ecosystems carry the same information backward, but that is a migration/backport mitigation rather than a reason to mark a backward-compatible base R6 alternative as available.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: An R4 extension can mitigate reverse-version loss, but it is not a less-breaking R6 base design.

evidence.detail: R6 defines `participant.supportingInfo` as `0..* Reference(Resource)`.
No R4 CareTeam element named `participant.supportingInfo` is present.

examples.examplesMd: A strict R4 CareTeam has no standard place for `supportingInfo`; an extension or external relationship is needed to avoid data loss.

findings.narrativeMd: `participant.supportingInfo` is a useful R6 addition but creates a reverse-version loss point. It is summary content and may be clinically or legally meaningful even though it is optional.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 validation is unaffected because old instances simply lack the new optional element. R6-to-R4 conversion is not lossless unless a cross-version extension or external link store is used.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: When converting R6 to R4, preserve `supportingInfo` using a documented extension or companion Provenance/Consent/DocumentReference relationship, and make consumers aware that the data is not a native R4 CareTeam field. Include test cases for arbitrary target resource types.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Because this is additive in R6, the main backward-compatible alternative is not a different R6 design but a shared extension for R4 compatibility. That extension would reduce data loss for mixed-version ecosystems.

findings.title: Example-bound category and participant-role ValueSet compositions changed

oldState.summary: R4 binds `category` and `participant.role` with example strength to care-team-category and participant-role ValueSets. The R4 ValueSets use LOINC/SNOMED filter-based compose definitions.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: R4 care-team-category uses LOINC `is-a` filters over eight LOINC answer-list concepts. R4 participant-role uses SNOMED CT `is-a` filters for concepts 125676002, 223366009, and 394730007.

oldState.narrativeMd: The R4 bindings are example strength, so they guide coding but do not constrain validation.

newState.summary: R6 keeps example-strength bindings but changes compose definitions: care-team-category enumerates eight LOINC concepts, and participant-role uses three explicit SNOMED concepts plus different SNOMED filters.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: R6 care-team-category explicitly lists LA27975-4, LA27976-2, LA27977-0, LA27978-8, LA28865-6, LA28866-4, LA27980-4, and LA28867-2. R6 participant-role includes explicit SNOMED CT codes 429577009, 116154003, and 133932002, retains an `is-a 223366009` filter, and changes another filter to `is-a 224930009`.

newState.narrativeMd: The binding strength remains example, but implementations that use these ValueSets for picklists, analytics normalization, or local profile derivation may see changed candidate codes.

facts.newValue: SNOMED explicit concepts 429577009, 116154003, 133932002 plus filters is-a 223366009 and 224930009

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The StructureDefinition binding canonicals are stable, but the versioned ValueSet resources in the two packages have different compose definitions.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Because both bindings are example strength, base FHIR validation should not reject instances solely for using codes outside the example sets. The practical risk is semantic and operational: applications that treat example bindings as picklists, preferred analytics groupers, or profile seeds may experience changed code availability.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Terminology guidance changes can affect categorization consistency but do not by themselves invalidate base CareTeam instances.

justification.inferredGoal: Refine example terminology guidance for CareTeam category and participant role.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Example binding changes do not make base R4 CareTeam instances invalid; expansion notes or ConceptMaps are migration aids.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The ValueSet compose definitions changed and no terminology expansions or narrative rationale were available, so the intended refinement cannot be fully assessed. However, the CareTeam bindings remain example strength, meaning base R4 instances should not become invalid solely because their category or role code is outside the R6 example ValueSet. The backward-compatible alternative field is therefore not applicable to base R4-to-R6 validation compatibility.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Publishing expansion comparisons, ConceptMaps, or historical notes would be useful migration guidance for systems that treated the example sets as picklists or profile seeds. Those artifacts do not constitute a less-breaking R6 base design alternative, and keeping the old compose definitions would mainly protect local conventions rather than preserve base-valid R4 instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Local picklists and derived profiles may need comparison, but that is not a base R4-to-R6 design break.

evidence.detail: R4 care-team-category uses multiple LOINC `is-a` filters.
R6 care-team-category explicitly enumerates eight LOINC concepts.
R4 participant-role uses SNOMED CT filters including `is-a 125676002`, `is-a 223366009`, and `is-a 394730007`.
R6 participant-role uses three explicit SNOMED CT concepts, keeps `is-a 223366009`, and uses `is-a 224930009`.

examples.examplesMd: No concrete old-valid/new-invalid code example is asserted because example bindings are not validation constraints and full terminology expansions were not computed.

findings.narrativeMd: The terminology guidance for category and participant role changed even though the CareTeam bindings remain example strength. This should not break base validation, but it can still break local conventions if systems generated UI choices, reports, or profile bindings from the core ValueSets.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Base R4 and R6 validators should not reject CareTeam instances merely because a category or role code is outside an example ValueSet. However, stricter local profiles derived from these ValueSets could reject different codes after migration. Without expansion comparison, the exact set-level delta is uncertain.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not assume local picklists generated from R4 example ValueSets are still aligned with R6 guidance. Run terminology-server expansions for the local SNOMED CT and LOINC versions, compare effective expansions, and update local profiles or ConceptMaps if users selected codes from portions no longer represented in R6.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: For example bindings, a backward-compatible migration story would publish explicit expansion comparisons or ConceptMaps rather than relying only on changed compose definitions. That would let implementers distinguish intended narrowing from representation cleanup.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Requires terminology review with licensed/current SNOMED CT and LOINC expansion behavior.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: The CareTeam canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, baseDefinition, derivation, and abstract flag are stable. The publication status changed from draft to active, which is noted separately but is not an identity break.
`CareTeam.status` remains a modifier because of `entered-in-error`. No retained local CareTeam element changed modifier semantics. Inherited `modifierExtension` snapshot differences are out of scope.
No fixed value, pattern value, or default value constraints were found on local CareTeam elements in either version.
No local CareTeam element introduced maxLength, regex, minValue, or maxValue restrictions in the compared definitions.
No local slicing definitions were found on CareTeam elements in either R4 or R6.

`CareTeam.status` remains required-bound to `care-team-status`, and the local CodeSystem has the same five codes and definitions in R4 and R6. `CareTeam.reason` keeps the clinical-findings example binding from the old reasonCode concept. Example binding ValueSet compose changes for category and participant role are covered as a finding.

No retained same-path local CareTeam element had a material summary-flag change. Summary payload still changes because R4 summary element `encounter` was removed and R6 summary element `participant.supportingInfo` was added.

No change was found to the resourceType identity or base JSON/XML representation rules. Serialization and code-generation breaks are limited to the changed local element names, choice element introduction, removed fields, and cardinality/type changes documented in findings.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: CareTeam StructureDefinition status changed from draft to active
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The canonical identity and content model correspondence remain stable; publication status does not by itself invalidate instances.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Governance processes may treat the R6 resource as more mature, but implementers should still account for ballot-build status of the package as a whole.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Root CareTeam description broadened from patient-focused planned participants to broader care coordination participants
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The root text changed, but retained structural elements already supported Patient or Group subjects and CareTeam participants in R4. The change is mainly semantic clarification and broadening.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Review user-facing descriptions and business rules that assume CareTeam is only for a single patient or only for planned future participants.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 added guidance on Patient versus Group subject use
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: `CareTeam.subject` remains `0..1 Reference(Patient|Group)` with unchanged cardinality and target profiles.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: The new comment says to use Group for care provision to all members of a group and Patient for individual care; local validation or UI guidance may want to surface this distinction.
